documents: Sharma, Mutz & Ehlers 2022, Earth Surf. Dynam. 10, 997-1015, published PDF
Publisher XML full text converted to located text (jats_text)

entry.evidence: by addressing the following hypothesis: if late Cenozoic global climate change resulted in latitudinal variations in ground surface temperatures

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: Names the gap: climate-change predictions have not been combined with process-based frost cracking models at global scale.
steps.quote: no study has taken full advantage of climate change predictions in conjunction with a process-based understanding of the spatiotemporal variations in frost cracking

steps.action: States the hypothesis: latitudinal changes in ground surface temperature should shift more intense frost cracking to lower latitudes in colder climates.
steps.quote: leads to the occurrence of more intense frost cracking at lower latitudes during colder climates

steps.action: Takes daily land-surface temperatures from the authors' own earlier ECHAM5 T159 time-slice simulations (PI, MH, LGM, PLIO), keeping 15 of 17 model years after spin-up.
steps.quote: This paper builds upon and uses paleoclimate model simulations we previously published for different time periods

steps.action: Uses present-day HWSD v1.2 soil thickness, upscaled to the GCM grid and held constant across all time slices because no paleo-soil data exist.
steps.quote: Soil thickness data were obtained from the re-gridded Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) v1.2

steps.action: Derives MAT and Ta from the GCM output and drives an analytical 1D heat-conduction solution with sinusoidal temperatures instead of GCM daily values; sets diffusivities, 20 m depth and 200 depth intervals.
steps.quote: we refrained from using daily paleotemperatures from Mutz et al. (2018) and instead use sinusoidal daily temperatures

steps.action: Runs three published FCI models (Anderson 1998; Hales and Roering 2007; Andersen et al. 2015) at each grid cell and differences each time slice against PI; presents Model 3 in the main text.
steps.quote: We applied three different approaches (models) with different levels of complexity to estimate global variations in frost cracking

steps.action: Designs two Model 3 experiments, with and without the distance-to-water penalty function, because its value is uncertain.
steps.quote: it is unclear if the inclusion of the penalty function leads to a better representation of frost cracking processes

steps.action: Model 3 Scenario 1 (with penalty), with glaciated regions masked: global FCI sum is highest in the LGM, then MH, then PI; FCI correlates strongly with Ta and weakly to moderately with MAT.
steps.quote: The predicted global sum of FCI is greatest for the LGM

steps.action: Checks the Scenario 1 PI and MH spatial pattern against Models 1 and 2 run on the same inputs (results in the Supplement).
steps.quote: This is consistent with results from Models 1 and 2 (see Supplement).

steps.action: Reruns Model 3 without the penalty function (Scenario 2): the global sum now peaks in the MH, and the LGM sum is the lowest.
steps.quote: we estimate global FCI distribution using Model 3 (Andersen et al., 2015) without applying the penalty function

steps.action: Compares global FCI sums from all models and scenarios with published glacial-interglacial weathering flux estimates (~20% higher in the LGM); only Scenario 1 matches.
steps.quote: are inconsistent with studies of global weathering fluxes during glacial and inter-glacial periods

steps.action: Concludes that the distance-to-water penalty function matters for global FCI estimates, which favours Scenario 1.
steps.quote: These results highlight the importance of the penalty function (i.e., dependency of FCI on distance to water) in first-order (global) estimations of FCI.

steps.action: Maps Model 3 FCI anomalies relative to PI for the globe, Europe, Tibet and South America, masking ice cover and, for PLIO, the Pleistocene ice extent.
steps.quote: Our results for Model 3 are presented as maps showing time-slice-specific FCI anomalies relative to the PI climate simulation

steps.action: Summarizes the anomalies (MH small; PLIO larger and more varied; LGM largest) and compares them with the climate anomalies of Mutz et al. (2018) and Mutz and Ehlers (2019).
steps.quote: The LGM simulation produced the greatest differences in FCI with respect to the PI simulation.

steps.action: Compares modelled FCI trends with previous studies (Rempel 2016 on Ta; Walder and Hallet 1985; Marshall 2015 and 2017 on the Oregon LGM; weathering fluxes) and finds broad consistency.
steps.quote: Taken together, previous studies are consistent with the broad trends in FCI predicted by our global analysis.

steps.action: Intercompares Models 1-3: the time slice with the largest global sum differs by model (PI, MH, LGM, MH), which the authors attribute to how each model treats water availability and soil cover.
steps.quote: The pattern of global sums in FCI values in specific time slices is different in all the three models

steps.action: Narrows the scope of the claim after listing limitations (constant soil thickness, uniform properties, coarse resolution, GCM inaccuracies): the results are maps of FCI sensitivity.
steps.quote: the results presented here are essentially maps of FCI sensitivity to climate change forcing

steps.action: Keeps the main findings: latitudinal extents per slice, small MH deviations, larger LGM and PLIO anomalies, and a 22% LGM increase in global FCI under Scenario 1.
steps.quote: Our models predict a global FCI increase of 22 % (relative to PI) in non-glaciated regions for this time period.

steps.action: Compares the predicted changes with the opening hypothesis and judges it not entirely confirmed.
steps.quote: [...] in FCI presented here do not entirely confirm our hypothesis

steps.action: Refines the hypothesis: FCI changes are not uniform at a given latitude, so spatial climate changes, not only latitudinal shifts, must be considered.
steps.quote: a more simplified approach of assuming only latitudinal shifts in FCI between cold and warm periods is not sufficient

end.claim: Driving Model 3 with ECHAM5 time slices, the LGM shows the largest FCI changes relative to PI (a 22% rise in global FCI in non-glaciated regions with the penalty function), the MH the smallest and the PLIO larger regional changes, so FCI shifts are regionally non-uniform rather than purely latitudinal.

decisive_move.sentence: Without forward-running the FCI models on the GCM time-slice temperatures, no paleo-FCI maps or anomalies would exist.

gates.evidence: A hypothesis is stated up front (§1 ¶3), but the key data (the ECHAM5 simulations) were inherited and not acquired to test it. The hypothesis could fail and was judged 'not entirely confirmed' (§6 ¶3); the headline FCI estimates faced only qualitative consistency checks against the literature (§5.1 ¶2, §5.3 ¶1). The paper reports nothing fixed before the outputs were seen, and the preference for Scenario 1 was set after comparing outputs with weathering flux studies.

imports.item: Analytical solution of the one-dimensional heat conduction equation with sinusoidal forcing
Pearson correlation with a 95% significance threshold

novelty_claims.quote: [...] knowledge, no study has taken full advantage of climate change predictions in conjunction with a process-based understanding
few studies have addressed how global climate change over the late Cenozoic may have impacted spatial variations in frost cracking intensity

limits: No review file or open discussion was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the paper thanks two anonymous referees. The Supplement (Models 1-2, Figs. S1-S2) was not supplied; the method checks against Models 1-2 are coded from main-text statements. Composition none_fits because the walk is a forward-model sensitivity study: a stated hypothesis, inherited simulations, and model variants compared against qualitative literature evidence. It is not trace_series, since no physical traces are observed, and not strong_inference, since there is no crucial test across rivals. No uncertainty bounds are given on FCI; resolution is set by the ~80 km GCM grid and the 5 km soil data, so estimate_with_resolution is generous. Sub-claims and their statuses: the latitudinal-shift hypothesis was not entirely confirmed (partly refuted, status none); the 22% LGM increase depends on choosing the penalty function (estimate, conditional on that auxiliary); the strong FCI-Ta correlation is a regularity within model output only (regularity_in_range). Inference: Scenario 1 was favoured after its output was seen to match the weathering flux studies, which is a post-hoc selection. The paper itself notes that the model's boundary-water assumption is inconsistent with Walder and Hallet (1985) (§5.3 ¶1); this is not coded as a disagreement because the paper does not dispute that work. Internal inconsistencies: the Model 1 diffusivity is 1.5×10^-7 (§3.2.1 ¶1) versus 1.5×10^-6 (§3.1 ¶2); the Figure 4 caption swaps the soil and bedrock porosities relative to Table 3; V_CW is said to be in 'Table 2' (it is in Table 3); §5.5 ¶1 cites 'Sect. 5.5' for the agreement with previous work (likely Sect. 5.3); Figure 5 labels Model 2 'Hales et al., 2005'.

disagreements.support: Cites physical models, field data and lab simulations that do not support a fixed FCW, yet the paper still applies it in all three models.
disagreements.quote: However, this assumption is not supported by physical models (e.g., Walder and Hallet, 1985), field data

disagreements.support: Replaces it with a value judged more representative for rocks in general; no comparison of effects is shown.

disagreements.target: FCI formulations without the distance-to-water penalty (Models 1-2; Model 3 Scenario 2)
disagreements.support: Their global sums imply less frost cracking in the LGM, contrary to published ~20% higher LGM weathering fluxes (Gibbs and Kump 1994; Ludwig et al. 1999).
disagreements.quote: are inconsistent with studies of global weathering fluxes during glacial and inter-glacial periods

alternatives_considered.alternatives: GCM daily paleotemperatures from Mutz et al. (2018)
alternatives_considered.reason: Daily GCM variations cannot be validated as well as seasonal or annual means; avoid overinterpretation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Present-day HWSD soil thickness, constant across all time slices
Model 3 (Andersen et al., 2015) presented in the main text
alternatives_considered.reason: Most recent and complex treatment of relevant processes, such as soil cover

alternatives_considered.chosen: Model 3 run both with and without the penalty function; Scenario 1 (with) favoured
alternatives_considered.reason: Unclear whether the penalty improves the representation; Scenario 1 later matched weathering flux studies

alternatives_considered.chosen: PLIO masked with the LGM or maximum Quaternary ice extent; PLIO global sum not compared
alternatives_considered.reason: The modern soil depth assumption is heavily violated there; the global sum could be heavily affected by masking

alternatives_considered.chosen: Uniform thermal diffusivity and porosity for bedrock and sediment worldwide
alternatives_considered.reason: Simplification; no global inventories of these properties
